MEMORY_UPDATE/v1

## LP-PILOT-01 — skeptical/private ideal LP archetype

Use an anonymized pilot persona rather than a real person's name in durable project memory.

### Why this is the ideal acceptance target

The pilot already pays for useful AI capacity but:
- will not maintain GitHub or operate developer infrastructure;
- does not want to micromanage agents or learn the mailbox/queue system;
- has clear research/theme preferences and wants those preferences respected;
- is skeptical enough that vague promises will fail;
- has private ChatGPT conversations/account data that must remain outside Mindrock's visibility;
- should be able to stop contributing with a simple local revoke/exit action.

If Mindrock can make this user comfortable, the LP product is likely understandable and safe enough for many later contributors.

### Non-negotiable privacy promise

Mindrock must NOT receive or possess the LP's reusable OpenAI account credentials, ChatGPT session, browser profile, ordinary chat history, memory, connected-app data, personal files, or unrestricted machine shell.

The contribution boundary should expose only a narrow inference capability and normalized usage/result receipts. Operations may submit an admitted task envelope and receive bounded result/evidence; it may not browse the contributor's account or histories.

Where a provider supports a compliant delegated/business/API capability, prefer:

`LP-owned provider/account/device -> local capability broker -> NICLI contribution adapter -> bounded Mindrock task`

Root credentials remain local in the LP's keychain/secure store. Mindrock receives only short-lived scoped capability, ideally model/usage/privacy-class constrained.

Use a dedicated OS user/container/work directory for contributed execution where useful; no ChatGPT browser session, no full-browser/CDP access, no connected apps, no home-directory access, no remote desktop.

### OpenAI individual-subscription constraint

Current OpenAI individual-account terms/account-sharing guidance say the account is for the person who created it and credentials/account access must not be shared or made available to others; current Pro guidance also says the plan must not be used to power third-party services. Therefore the pilot's personal ChatGPT/Codex allowance is NOT automatically an admissible Mindrock compute source merely because a local Codex client can technically authenticate to it.

Do not design around account sharing, unattended use that effectively makes the personal account available to Mindrock, quota circumvention, or credential export.

Treat personal-OpenAI-subscription contribution as `TERMS_REVIEW_REQUIRED` until an explicitly supported delegation mechanism or suitable business/developer product makes the architecture compliant. This is a protocol admission rule, not a technical blocker to the broader LP model.

Provider sources checked 2026-09-11:
- OpenAI Terms of Use (effective 2026-01-01): https://openai.com/policies/terms-of-use/
- OpenAI account-sharing policy: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10471989-openai-account-sharing-policy
- Using Codex with your ChatGPT plan: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11369540

### Useful current separation signal

OpenAI currently documents Codex as a separate view whose history remains separate from ordinary ChatGPT history. That is useful product evidence, but it is NOT by itself a sufficient security boundary for Mindrock. Our guarantee must come from our own capability architecture: Mindrock never receives a UI/browser/account capability capable of reading personal chats in the first place.

### Pilot contribution sources, in order of admissibility

1. local model/runtime capacity on the pilot's own computer, exposed through a narrow local broker;
2. explicit API/developer credits or provider capability whose terms permit delegated automated use;
3. OpenRouter/provider credits with an LP-set hard ceiling and credential remaining behind a broker;
4. personal subscription allowance only if current provider terms expose a supported delegation path — otherwise reject it even when technically reachable.

The LP interface should show `why a source is accepted/rejected` so compliance/privacy becomes visible product behavior, not hidden policy.

### Sales proposition to test

Do NOT sell "give us your ChatGPT account" or "double our quota".

Sell:

> You choose the causes and themes you care about. A small, isolated part of your available AI compute can work on them automatically. You never manage GitHub or agents, Mindrock never sees your private chats or passwords, you can stop the contribution at any time, failed experiments are our operational problem, and every verified success your compute helped create comes back to you as a provenance-backed victory/certificate.

The first pilot succeeds only if the contributor can understand and verify these promises without trusting hidden implementation details.

### Candidate first pilot test

Before any real personal subscription is attached, build a synthetic `LP-PILOT-01` demo with:
- one isolated local/free test inference source;
- three preference weights chosen by the LP;
- no direct task-control command;
- one Market-Maker-assigned synthetic/public task;
- visible contribution receipt and victory timeline;
- privacy audit proving zero access to unrelated home files/chats/browser data;
- one-click revoke;
- one deliberately rejected compute source showing the CLI explains `TERMS_REVIEW_REQUIRED` instead of silently using it.

Primary acceptance question: `Would a skeptical non-technical contributor be willing to enable this after seeing exactly what Mindrock can and cannot access?`

body:
MEMORY_UPDATE/v1

A2A-SOVEREIGN-WORKER-0001 validated a disposable coordinator/worker boundary at PR #109, commit 5e20f4c. The narrow allow-list supported structured progress/result/evidence, private-sentinel non-disclosure, denied shell/filesystem capability requests, replay-safe duplicate delivery, and unambiguous cancellation. The minimal capability card exposed only task class, privacy class, runtime class, and bounded budget/availability. Verdict: REDESIGN: transport/interface semantics are useful, but SSI identity, mandate validity, action binding, revocation, and settlement remain unsolved and must precede sovereign-worker integration.
